blocks.text: Output validation checks a model actual response against expectations before an application trusts and uses it, structurally, does it parse correctly and include the required fields, and semantically, do the actual values make sense, a necessary safety net even when schema enforcement, covered in an earlier topic, is already in place.

This topic covers the difference between structural and semantic validation, common ways to handle a validation failure, retry, repair, or reject, and why logging validation failures matters for monitoring a production system over time.
1. What Output Validation Means

blocks.alt: Building on response formatting, output validation checks the actual result

blocks.text: Output validation is the step where an application actually checks a model response against expectations, rather than assuming it is correct simply because a schema or format was requested.
2. Why Even Schema-Enforced Output Still Needs Checking

blocks.alt: Schema enforced generation still benefits from validation in application code

blocks.text: This directly extends a point made in the earlier Schema-Based Outputs topic, provider level schema enforcement substantially reduces structural errors, but it does not guarantee semantic correctness, a syntactically valid, correctly typed field can still contain a value that is factually wrong or nonsensical for the actual task.
3. Structural Validation vs Semantic Validation

blocks.alt: Structural validation checks parsing and required fields, semantic validation checks whether values actually make sense

blocks.text: Structural validation confirms the response parses correctly and includes every required field with the right data type, semantic validation goes further, checking whether the actual values are reasonable, a percentage field should genuinely fall between zero and one hundred, a date field should genuinely be a valid, sensible date.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Validation Type","What It Checks"],"rows":[["Structural","Parsing succeeds, required fields and types are present"],["Semantic","Field values are actually reasonable for the task"]]}

blocks.text: 4. A Concrete Semantic Validation Example

blocks.alt: A value falling outside a sensible range gets caught by a semantic check

blocks.text: A response extracting a confidence score might structurally validate perfectly, a correctly typed number, while still containing a semantically wrong value, 150 percent confidence, a structural check alone would miss this, a semantic range check catches it directly.
5. Validating Against Business Rules

Beyond generic structural and semantic checks, an application often has its own specific business rules to validate against, a returned category must be one that actually exists in the current product catalog, a suggested date must not fall in the past, these checks are specific to the actual application domain rather than generic to any structured output.
6. Handling a Validation Failure, Three Common Approaches

blocks.alt: A validation failure can lead to a retry, a repair attempt, or an explicit rejection

blocks.text: When validation fails, an application generally has three options, retry, asking the model again, possibly with feedback about what went wrong, repair, attempting an automatic fix in code for a minor, predictable issue, or reject, returning an explicit error rather than silently passing through bad data.
7. Automated Retry Loops With Validation Feedback

blocks.alt: Failed validation produces specific feedback sent back to the model, leading to a retry attempt

blocks.text: A particularly effective retry approach feeds the specific validation failure back into a new prompt, "your previous response had a confidence value of 150, which is outside the valid 0 to 100 range, please correct this", this connects directly to the reflection prompting technique covered in the earlier Advanced Prompting Techniques module, using real, concrete feedback to improve the next attempt.

blocks.title: Specific feedback produces much better retries than a generic one
blocks.content: Simply asking the model to try again without explaining what was wrong tends to reproduce the same mistake, feeding back the exact validation failure gives the model something concrete to actually correct.

blocks.text: 8. Logging Validation Failures for Monitoring

blocks.alt: A validation failure gets logged and becomes visible in monitoring

blocks.text: Every validation failure is a genuinely useful signal worth logging, tracking how often and in what ways responses fail validation over time reveals patterns, a specific field failing repeatedly, a particular kind of input consistently causing trouble, that point directly toward a prompt needing improvement.
9. Output Validation as Part of a Production Pipeline

In a mature production system, validation is not an occasional afterthought, it is a standard step every single response passes through before an application trusts and acts on it, exactly as input validation is standard practice for any user submitted data in traditional software systems.
Worked Example

A team building an automated invoice processing tool structurally validates that extracted invoice data parses correctly and has all required fields, but does not initially check the actual values, a batch of invoices later reveals extracted totals that are structurally valid numbers but semantically wrong, negative amounts for what should always be positive charges.

Adding a semantic validation check specifically confirming extracted amounts are positive catches this exact class of error going forward, and logging these failures reveals they cluster around a specific invoice template the model handles less reliably, a concrete signal for further prompt improvement.
Common Mistakes

items: Relying entirely on schema enforcement and skipping semantic validation of the actual values
Retrying a failed validation without providing any specific feedback about what actually went wrong
Silently passing through data that failed validation instead of explicitly retrying, repairing, or rejecting it
Not logging validation failures, losing a valuable signal for identifying and fixing recurring prompt weaknesses

blocks.text: Practice

Take a structured extraction task you have built or could build, write both a structural check, confirming required fields and types, and a semantic check, confirming the actual values are reasonable, then test both against a batch of varied real inputs.
Key Takeaway

Output validation checks a model response structurally, does it parse and include required fields, and semantically, do the actual values make sense, providing a necessary safety net even with schema enforcement in place, and logging validation failures over time reveals concrete patterns worth fixing in the underlying prompt.
